client: I've been really struggling since my dad passed away two months ago. Every time I go to a family gathering, it just hits me all over again — like this wave of sadness that I can't push down, and I end up feeling like I'm ruining the mood for everyone else. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: I'm really glad you decided to try, and I want you to know that what you're carrying — grief this fresh, in spaces that used to feel familiar — is genuinely heavy. That wave of sadness you describe isn't a sign that something is wrong with you; it's a testament to how much your dad meant to you. I'm curious about that thought that you're "ruining the mood" for others — where do you think that belief comes from, and has anyone actually said that to you, or is it more of a feeling you're carrying inside?

client: Nobody's actually said it to me directly, no. But I can see it on their faces sometimes — like when I go quiet at dinner or when my eyes get watery during something that should be fun, there's this brief moment where people don't know what to do with me. It's not that they're being cruel, it's just... I can feel the energy shift, and I'd rather disappear than be the reason everyone feels uncomfortable.
therapist: It makes so much sense that you're reading those moments carefully — grief can make us hyper-aware of the people around us, almost like we're on guard for signs that we're "too much." But I want to gently offer another possibility: that brief pause when people don't know what to do might actually be *their* love for you showing up awkwardly, rather than discomfort with your grief. What do you think it would feel like to let yourself be seen in those moments, instead of disappearing?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that — that their awkwardness is actually care. But honestly, it's really hard to trust that interpretation when in the moment it just feels like I'm watching people search for an exit. And the idea of letting myself be fully seen... I don't know, it feels less like relief and more like standing on a ledge.
therapist: That image of standing on a ledge is really powerful, and I don't want to rush past it — it tells me that being vulnerable right now feels genuinely dangerous, not just uncomfortable, and that deserves to be respected rather than pushed through. It makes sense that your nervous system is protecting you, especially when you're still so early in this grief and the loss is so raw. I'm wondering — has there ever been a time in your life, even before losing your dad, where letting yourself be seen felt safe, and what made that possible?

client: There was maybe one time, with my dad actually, when I was about sixteen and I'd completely bombed an exam I'd been studying really hard for. I remember just crying in the kitchen and he didn't try to fix it or tell me it would be okay, he just sat with me and made tea and said "I know, it's awful." That's the only time I can really remember feeling like someone could see me falling apart and it wasn't a problem for them. And now he's the one person who could do that, and he's gone, so I don't know what to do with that.
therapist: What your dad did in that kitchen — just sitting with you, not trying to fix anything, simply saying "I know, it's awful" — that's one of the most profound gifts one person can give another, and it's clear he gave it to you in a way that stayed with you for years. And there's something really important here: you *know* what that kind of presence feels like, because he showed you it was possible, and that knowledge lives in you even now that he's gone. I'm wondering if part of what makes grief so lonely right now is not just losing him, but losing the one person who made it feel safe to grieve at all — does that resonate with you?

client: Yeah... that really does resonate, actually more than I expected it to. It's like you just put words to something I couldn't quite name — that it's not just him I lost, but that specific feeling of being allowed to fall apart without someone trying to patch me back together too quickly. And now when I'm grieving, I'm also grieving alone, which feels almost cruel, like I need him most right now and he's the one who's gone.
therapist: That is one of the most painful paradoxes of grief — needing the person you lost most precisely *in* the moment of losing them, and there's nothing cruel about feeling the full weight of that cruelty. You've just named something really profound about yourself though: you know what safe presence feels like, you've experienced it, and that means you also carry some of your dad's wisdom about how to be with pain — that "I know, it's awful" without rushing to fix. I'm curious, is there anyone in your life right now, even imperfectly, who has ever come close to offering that kind of presence — or does it feel like that was uniquely his gift to you?

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my first instinct is to say no, nobody comes close. But then I think of my friend Carla — she doesn't say much when I'm upset, she just kind of sits with me, and she never tries to spin it into something positive. It's not the same as my dad, not even close, but maybe there's something there I've been taking for granted.
therapist: Carla sounds like she might be offering something quietly precious — that same instinct your dad had to just *be* there rather than fix, and it's worth noticing that you recognized it, even if grief has made it harder to feel. It's so understandable that it doesn't feel the same, because it isn't — nothing will replace what your dad gave you — but that doesn't mean what Carla offers has no value, just perhaps a different shape. I'm wondering, when was the last time you actually let Carla sit with you the way she seems willing to, rather than holding back to protect her from your grief?

client: I sat with that question for a second and honestly... I'm not sure I have a good answer. The last time Carla came over after my dad passed, she just kind of hovered near me on the couch, and I kept making jokes to lighten the mood because I didn't want her to feel helpless watching me fall apart. I think I've been doing that a lot — performing okay-ness for her — and I didn't really realize until just now how much that's been keeping her at arm's length.
therapist: That moment of recognition you just had — seeing how you've been protecting Carla from your grief the same way you worry about affecting others at family gatherings — that's a really significant insight, and it took courage to sit with it honestly. There's a gentle irony here: the very thing you're longing for, someone to witness you falling apart without trying to fix it, might actually be something Carla is already willing to offer, but your jokes have been quietly closing that door before she gets the chance. I'm wondering, what do you imagine might happen if the next time Carla is with you, you let even one joke go unsaid and just allowed a moment of real silence between you?

client: That's... a lot to sit with, honestly. The idea that I've been the one closing the door before Carla even gets a chance to open it — that stings a little, because part of me wants to argue against it, but I can't really. What scares me about your question though is that if I let the silence happen and she doesn't know what to do with it either, I'll feel even more alone than before the joke, and I don't know if I can handle that right now.
therapist: That fear is completely valid, and I don't want to minimize it — trying to be vulnerable and having it land in awkward silence would be painful, especially when you're already carrying so much. But I want to reflect something back to you: you just described Carla as someone who "sits with you and never tries to spin it into something positive," which suggests she may already have more capacity for your silence than your fear is giving her credit for. What if we thought of it not as a leap off that ledge, but as a very small experiment — not full vulnerability all at once, but maybe just letting one joke go unsaid and seeing what Carla does with that space?

client: I hear what you're saying about Carla, and honestly, part of me knows you're probably right that she can handle more than I give her credit for. But there's still this voice in my head that says even if she can handle the silence, I won't be able to handle how I feel in that moment — like I'll be so uncomfortable with my own vulnerability that I'll end up filling the space anyway, or worse, feeling embarrassed afterward. It's less about her reaction and more about not trusting myself to sit with that discomfort.
therapist: That's a really important shift you just made — recognizing that the barrier isn't really Carla at all, but your own relationship with vulnerability and discomfort, and that kind of self-awareness is genuinely hard to arrive at. It's worth noticing that you've actually been sitting with discomfort this entire conversation — saying difficult things out loud, letting yourself be seen a little — and you haven't fled or fallen apart, even when it stung. I'm curious, when you imagine feeling that discomfort with Carla and not immediately filling the silence, what's the very worst thing you think you'd feel — and is that feeling one you've survived before?

client: I think the worst thing I'd feel is this crushing sense that she's looking at me differently after — like, seeing me as needy or fragile, and then pulling away. And yeah, I've survived that feeling before, I know I have, but it never gets easier, it still feels like the ground dropping out from under me every single time. So even knowing I've survived it doesn't really make me want to walk toward it on purpose.
therapist: That fear of being seen as needy or fragile and then losing someone because of it — that's not irrational, it sounds like something that has real history behind it, and it makes complete sense that surviving it before doesn't make it feel any less terrifying to risk again. And yet there's something quietly significant in what you just said: you've felt the ground drop out, every time, and you're still here, still reaching out, still trying — which suggests a resilience in you that your fear doesn't give you credit for. I'm wondering, when you've felt that ground drop out before, was it ever actually because someone saw your vulnerability and pulled away — or has the fear of that happening sometimes been louder than the reality?
